Abaya : l’obsession française qui affect: Abaya: the French obsession affecting Quebec women
Comment expliquer qu’une querelle frança: How did a French quarrel make its way here, and what are the consequences?
Des jeunes femmes musulmanes québécoises: Young Muslim women from Quebec and France. Illustration: Nia E-K
En France, la sphère politico-médiatique: In France, the political and media sphere regularly questions how Muslim women dress. The latest controversy centres on <l1>the abaya</l1>. At the start of the school year, France’s minister of National Education banned the wearing of these long dresses in public schools (which serve students aged 11 to 18).
Au Québec, de nombreuses femmes craignen: In Quebec, many women fear this controversy will affect them… when it isn’t already doing so. How did a French quarrel make its way here, and what are the consequences? We chose to hand the mic to those most affected.
<strong>« T’es au Québec ici, t’es pas e: “You’re in Quebec, you’re not in Afghanistan!”
Nous avons rencontré Sarah**, une Montré: We met Sarah**, a Montrealer who has worn the abaya for two years. On September 11, the 24-year-old was getting ready to meet a friend for a shopping trip. As usual, she slipped on one of her long dresses. She picked the one she had just bought, an elegant, good-quality piece, she says.
Moins de 15 minutes plus tard, au pied d: Less than 15 minutes later, at the foot of her building, Sarah was assaulted in the street. “You’re in Quebec, you’re not in Afghanistan!” yelled a man who appeared Caucasian. He pointed at her, accompanying the gesture with “fuck you” and other insults. She remembers that no one around her reacted.
« [Après ça], j’ai pris le bus en direct: “[After that], I took the bus toward the metro. The whole way, I was so anxious, I asked myself: ‘Should I turn around and go home?’ But I kept telling myself: ‘No, be strong.’ So I called my husband, and I stayed on the line with him until I got to my destination. I was deeply shaken.”
Sarah est catégorique : elle voit dans c: Sarah is adamant: she sees a direct link between this assault and the controversy stirring up France. “I’ve been wearing abayas, these long, loose dresses, for two years now,” explains the veiled woman. “But these past two weeks have been especially gruelling. People’s heavy, insistent stares have become constant, like little stings that assail me all day long. It wasn’t like this before. Now I feel like I’m under constant surveillance.”
Pour comprendre ce qui se trame au Québe: To understand what is happening in Quebec, a quick look back at the affair currently inflaming the French media is in order. At a press conference for the start of the school year, France’s minister of National Education, Gabriel Attal, described this dress – the literal translation of the word “abaya,” which can also refer to a coat – as a Muslim religious garment. He said it had “no place” in French schools. This garment, which <l1>is not actually religious</l1>, is now coded as such, and any collège or lycée student (so roughly 11 to 18 years old) who wears it risks disciplinary action.
Pour comprendre la situation en France,: To understand the situation in France, let’s start by explaining what an abaya is. Originally, it was a short, sleeveless coat, worn regardless of sex or religion, notably by the Bedouin. Today, the abaya is a long, loose dress, popular in various regions, including North Africa and Southwest Asia. It is appreciated for its modesty and worn mainly by women. It comes in many colours and styles, and can even be found in collections from popular brands like Zara and Dolce Gabbana.
Dans l’Hexagone, de nombreux membres de: In France, many opposition members have denounced what they call a political manoeuvre. The controversy, they say, conveniently sweeps underlying problems under the rug: teacher shortages, job insecurity, overwork, underfunded schools… The damage is done, however: the French government has trained the cameras on the <l1>298 girls</l1> who showed up in an abaya on the first day of school, or 0.006% of students***.
Ainsi, début septembre, des jeunes femme: And so, in early September, young women were met by supervisors, teachers and school administrators who judged whether or not their outfits were religious. In other words, the intention behind the length of their dress. In the process, girls wearing <l1>jeans with a fitted sweater and a kimono</l1>, <l2>matching loose jumpsuits</l2>, or even an <l3>outfit deemed too dark</l3> were refused entry to class.
Quel est le risque lié à une telle mesur: What is the risk of such a measure, according to those who oppose it? Sociologist<l1> Hanane Karimi</l1> fears a slide toward discrimination based on appearance or surname: “What isn’t being said is that something ethnocultural is a strong indicator in how people judge whether it’s an abaya or a long dress.”
<strong>Pourquoi une polémique française: Why would a French controversy resonate in Quebec?
Zeinab Diab rédige actuellement une thès: Zeinab Diab is currently writing a thesis in religious studies at the Institut d’études religieuses of the Université de Montréal on the effect of Bill 21 on Muslim women. The researcher believes the measure against abayas, decreed in the name of secularism, has a strong chance of finding an echo in Quebec.
Se décrivant comme « l’enfant de la loi: Describing herself as “a child of Bill 101 and an adult of Bill 21,” Ms. Diab believes that neither Quebec nor France respects the principles of secularism.
« Le premier pilier de la laïcité est la: “The first pillar of secularism is the separation of state and churches, and the autonomy of religious bodies from political power,” she says. “From that flows the second principle, state neutrality, which stipulates that the state must neither impose nor directly or indirectly hinder a religion, and that it must not promote the interests of a majority or minority group either. The third pillar: secularism should not be a constraint on religion, but rather a way of living one’s faith. Finally, the fourth fundamental principle is equal treatment of all citizens,” she lists.
En France, la laïcité a été définie par: In France, secularism was defined by <l1>the 1905 law</l1>. In Canada, it is rather through the mention of “freedom of religion” in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms <l2>(section 2(a))</l2>. Along with several Supreme Court of Canada precedents**** that address the various principles of secularism.
En 2004, lors de l’introduction de la <l: In 2004, with the introduction of the law banning students in France from wearing religious symbols, a new form of secularism emerged. Historian Jean Baubérot calls it falsified secularism. In his view, the spirit of the 1905 law is no longer respected, because the young women targeted are now asked to hide their religiosity. Yet that law was originally created to guarantee freedom of religion.
Au sujet des risques de dérive au Québec: On the risk of a similar drift in Quebec, Ms. Diab says the province “takes a lot of inspiration from France.” She then adds: “Because of its minority situation (…), it relentlessly seeks to define itself. So it distinguishes itself in particular through its rejection of Canadian secularism, illustrated by Bill 21.”
Elle attire d’ailleurs l’attention sur u: She also draws attention to a revealing semantic quirk: in English, Bill 21 is titled “An Act Respecting the Laicity of the State.” Yet, the researcher explains, the word “laicity” is not common. Its use here is meant to set it apart from “secularism” and to promote the new French-style secularism. “So, as in France, Quebec defines itself by controlling its internal minority populations, within the imaginary borders of what constitutes the Quebec nation,” she adds.
<strong>Comment la législation anti-voil: How is French anti-veil legislation being exported to Belle Province?
Pour comprendre ce phénomène, nous avons: To understand this phenomenon, we consulted Professor Roshan Jahangeer. Her research looks at how anti-veil laws circulate between France and Quebec.
Selon elle, « des politiciens, des exper: According to her, “well-known politicians, experts and journalists” have travelled between the two countries to, among other things, argue in favour of enacting these laws or to cover their application. A trend that is still ongoing, she believes.
En décembre 2013, par exemple, une renco: In December 2013, for example, a meeting took place at the Élysée Palace in Paris between Pauline Marois, then leader of the Parti québécois and premier of Quebec, and the French president at the time, François Hollande. Initially devoted to trade and the electrification of transportation, the meeting quickly took a different turn when the subject of secularism came up in the context of the <l1>Charter of Quebec Values</l1>.
François Hollande affirme alors que « <l: François Hollande then stated that “<l1>secularism does not belong to France</l1>.” On the contrary, he said, “it is a principle, a value that we believe we can share with other countries and that makes it possible to live together […]. With Quebec, it is true that we also have common foundations that help explain why we may arrive at the same results.” Regarding this meeting, Pauline Marois also said she was “inspired” by the French president’s remarks.
Mme Jahangeer évoque également l’influen: Ms. Jahangeer also points to the influence of commentators like Mathieu Bock-Côté – who wrote a <l1>column</l1> on the abaya ban. “[He] is a Quebec columnist and a public figure whose influence is notable. He is currently based in France, which gives him his perspective on debates about secularism. His political opinions influence the Quebec public scene, where he is seen as a spokesperson for French-style secularism in Quebec,” she explains.
Mathieu Bock-Côté et Pauline Marois util: Mathieu Bock-Côté and Pauline Marois also use the same vocabulary and the same rhetoric as in France, despite a very different historical and sociocultural context. Consider the influence of the Church in Quebec public life, which persisted until the late 1960s, or the question of Islamist movements, which are not established in Quebec the way they are in France. Yet, the researcher notes, “terms like ‘living together,’ ‘gender equality,’ ‘feminism,’ ‘oppression,’ ‘Islamism,’ ‘progressive’ always come up when the subject of secularism is raised in the two francophone nations.”
L’universitaire estime aussi que c’est e: The academic also believes that silencing Muslim women creates a climate conducive to the birth of laws that oppose the wearing of the veil – a constant observed in both places. In France, “on debate shows, veiled Muslim women are frequently discussed without being given the opportunity to speak on set,” she notes.
La chercheuse Khaoula Zoghlami a d’aille: Researcher Khaoula Zoghlami analyzed the testimonies of Muslim women during the parliamentary hearings on Bill 21. Of 36 participants, only 3 women identified as Muslim were able to speak. “The speaking time given to these women who wear headscarves accounted for only 4.4% of the witnesses’ total speaking time. The percentage drops to 0.6% if you count only the speaking time of the one witness directly affected by the application of the bill, Ms. Bouchra Chelbi, a high school teacher.” By contrast, terms associated with Muslim women’s dress (hijab, niqab, veil, headscarf and burqa) were repeated 296 times, representing 73.8% of all terms used to refer to religious symbols.
Ce tableau apparaît dans l’étude de Khao: This table appears in Khaoula Zoghlami’s study titled <l1>Who Can Testify? Unwelcome Presence and Speech Under Surveillance</l1>. It highlights the repetition of words referring to religious symbols during the parliamentary consultation.
Le scénario d’un Québec qui interdirait: But is it conceivable that Quebec would ban the veil in schools? “Quebec is already on that path,” says Ms. Jahangeer. “It is a few years behind France, but it is nonetheless on its way to establishing a restrictive secularism.”
Zeinab Diab estime pour sa part que le Q: For her part, Zeinab Diab believes that Quebec and France demand that Muslim women remain invisible. “In the end, they are treated as second-class citizens,” says the Quebecer, who is herself Muslim and veiled.
Mais, dans l’immédiat, quelles répercuss: But in the immediate term, what repercussions does the French controversy have in Quebec’s school system?
Une mère rapporte que, le 6 septembre de: One mother reports that on September 6, she was informed by Collège Citoyen, a private high school in Laval, that wearing the veil and other religious symbols would be banned starting September 11. Students launched an online petition, which gathered nearly <l1>6,900 signatures</l1>, to denounce the fact that the administration “[had] gone so far as to personally approach veiled students and others wearing a cross to warn them that if they didn’t remove them by Friday, September 8, they would be expelled from school.”
L’établissement scolaire <l1>nie catégor: The school <l1>categorically denies</l1> having banned the veil. The administration says the message was misinterpreted and that its dress code has not changed since 2007. In a <l2>statement issued</l2> on September 8, Collège Citoyen said it was the victim of a campaign damaging its reputation. The administration explains that parents must submit an exemption request for the wearing of religious symbols, something the student’s mother had not been told. Other non-Muslim parents have criticized this exemption request. The school’s principal assured that students would not be expelled and held an open house to answer parents’ questions.
Mme Diab juge que cela est symptomatique: Ms. Diab considers this symptomatic. “It is a critical incident that reveals a fear increasingly taking hold in Muslim communities, given Quebec’s political climate, the enactment of Bill 21, and the fact that Quebec draws inspiration from French-style secularism and the social policies surrounding the control and discipline of Muslim women’s bodies.”
Parmi les centaines de commentaires form: Among the hundreds of comments left on this petition, it is clear that many signatories reject secularism as it is currently applied in France
<strong>Comment les Québécoises de confe: How Muslim women in Quebec are experiencing all this
Pour Sarah, les souvenirs de cette matin: For Sarah, memories of that mid-September morning continue to haunt her. “These past two weeks [since the announcement of this directive] have been especially gruelling. People’s heavy, insistent stares have become constant, like little stings that assail me all day long. It wasn’t like this before, and suddenly I feel like I’m under constant surveillance,” she says. “[Before leaving that day], I looked at myself in the mirror and wondered if something was wrong, if I should change my outfit, if I should choose something else. Then I told myself: ‘Why am I thinking about this now? I’ve never felt this before.’ Usually, I get dressed and head out without thinking much about it. And it was only a few minutes later, on my own street, that the assault happened.”
«Oui, c’est de la peur, mais en même tem: “Yes, it’s fear, but at the same time, nothing guarantees me that this kind of thing won’t happen again. So I prefer to stay home,” says the young woman.
Meriem*****, une autre jeune Québécoise: Meriem*****, another young Quebecer who has worn the hijab for a decade, is outraged: “There’s a lot of frustration, of anger at the absurdity of this directive [in France]. Even though I’m not French, a community is like a body, and when one organ suffers, the whole body suffers. I’ve been lucky not to have experienced anything since the September controversy, but I remain on my guard,” she explains.
Elle se remémore son expérience lorsque: She recalls her experience when Bill 21 was enacted. In a resigned tone, she says: “It’s as if I was being told: ‘You’re no longer part of society.’ When Bill 21 passed, I went through a collapse compounded by societal rejection. If Bill 21 made me feel that way, I can’t even imagine the suffering they’re enduring. ”
Shaheen Junaid, trésorière du chapitre m: Shaheen Junaid, treasurer of the Montréal chapter of the Canadian Council of Muslim Women, expresses her exhaustion with interminable debates. “I’m so sick of discussing what I put on my head instead of what’s in my head!” she exclaims. She regrets the decisions of the CAQ government. She says she is convinced that Quebecers will eventually feel the fallout of the abaya affair. “It feels like an old trap: first France, then Quebec. Whatever they do, we have to do it, you know – it’s like a little brother following his older sibling.”
Elle encourage toutefois les femmes musu: She nonetheless encourages Muslim women not to give up. “Don’t be afraid. This is your country. (…) You deserve to feel safe. You belong here, no matter what the law says.”
<strong>« L’abaya, un cocon où je peux ê: “The abaya, a cocoon where I can be myself”
Ici, au Québec, des Québécoises de confe: Here in Quebec, Muslim women are resisting this truncated secularism. Some, in a show of solidarity with their French sisters, have <l1>proudly worn abayas and kimonos</l1> in recent days.
Alors que la France se lance dans un déb: As France launches into a heated debate over the abaya and what it means, we would like to conclude by giving the floor to the women concerned. We are sharing the testimony of a Muslim woman who took part in Zeinab Diab’s research on the effect of Bill 21. This woman expressed her feelings about the abaya several months ago, well before the garment became the symbol of a divided francophonie. Here is her testimony:
« On connaît tous ce sentiment parfois d: “We all know that feeling sometimes of not wanting to get dressed, of taking our time, right? That’s when we opt for something simpler, like an abaya. Unfortunately, in public space, simply wearing an abaya can now be associated with religious extremism, even terrorism. Going to the supermarket can sometimes feel like a threat, even for perfectly normal, everyday activities.
« Pour ma part, (lorsque je porte une ab: “For my part, (when I wear an abaya), I no longer feel the pressure to please and conform to preset standards of physical beauty… Wearing the veil and loose clothing gives me great comfort. It means I don’t have to worry about following draconian diets. I don’t need to match the stereotypes of the woman with the perfect body all the time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. My choice of clothing gives me a feeling of comfort, a cocoon where I can simply be myself.”
